content: Ep 142: Astronomers report the first strong evidence for an exomoon orbiting a planet 73 light-years away.
Ep 141: Hubble has found the first “missing” black hole inside a famous star cluster by combining two decades of data with new infrared views.
Ep 140: A candidate Jupiter-sized moon orbiting far beyond our solar system is forcing astronomers to redraw the line between planets and moons.
Ep 139: A European spacecraft just cleared its final major test before hunting Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars.
Ep 138: Astronomers have watched a distant galaxy's central black hole erupt for the first time in real time after two prior outbursts went unseen until they faded.
Ep 137: Fifty years after Viking 1 touched down on Mars, new missions are shifting focus from the surface to the thin air above the Red Planet.
Ep 136: NASA's Psyche spacecraft just used Mars as a gravitational slingshot, returning a rich dataset that will sharpen its approach to a metal world never visited before.
Ep 135: A private Indian rocket just reached orbit on its first try while a NASA probe wakes up billions of miles out.
Ep 134: Astronomers report signs of an atmosphere on a rocky world in the habitable zone 48 light-years away, a first for planets of its kind.
Ep 133: Astronomers have directly imaged a third giant planet in the Beta Pictoris system by spotting its carbon monoxide signature with JWST.
Ep 132: China's Tianwen-2 probe has reached a near-Earth asteroid after a billion-kilometre chase, raising the possibility that the target is a long-lost lunar fragment.
Ep 131: Four new NASA missions will help turn the Moon into a permanent base while another rover just ran a full marathon on Mars.
Ep 130: A Chinese probe has reached a quasi-moon while JWST reveals a hot Jupiter with violently different day and night sides.
Ep 129: UN records now let anyone track satellite registrations that official sites still hide.
Ep 128: Japan just completed the first test flight of an experimental reusable rocket, landing it safely after launch.
Ep 127: A Chinese rocket just became only the second booster ever recovered after an orbital launch, landing on a barge after sending its payload skyward.
Ep 126: A Falcon 9 booster has now completed its 36th flight and landing, carrying 29 more Starlink satellites into orbit.
Ep 125: A total solar eclipse will turn day to night across northern Spain next month as the Moon fully covers the Sun.
Ep 124: Euclid telescope has found the two oldest quasars known, their light crossing more than 13 billion years to reach us.
Ep 123: An asteroid set for a once-in-a-millennium Earth flyby could be seen by ninety percent of the world's population.
Ep 122: Astronomers just found giant planets lighter than cotton candy, forcing a rethink of how worlds assemble.
Ep 121: A robotic spacecraft just launched to nudge a long-running NASA observatory back into a stable orbit.
Ep 120: A planet 25 light-years away shows signs it could support liquid water on its surface.
Ep 119: A shoebox-sized probe will soon ride an asteroid flyby to test surface operations before the rock skims Earth in 2029.
Ep 118: NASA is weighing whether to send a spare Mars rover to the Moon while awarding nearly $600 million in new lunar lander contracts.
Ep 117: NASA is launching a robot to lift its aging Swift telescope before atmospheric drag pulls it down.

content: Ep 123: Saudi Arabia’s strike on Yemen’s main port raises the risk of wider disruption to Red Sea shipping that carries fuel and goods for millions across the Middle East and beyond.
Ep 122: New U.S. tariffs of 10-12.5% on imports from 60 countries will raise costs for many goods and affect trade worldwide.
Ep 121: The United States has signed a landmark nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia, reshaping energy ties and non-proliferation rules across the Middle East.
Ep 120: Ukraine names a new army chief as shipping firms add fees over Hormuz risks and UK inflation eases to 2.6 percent.
Ep 119: U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods and a major rescue in India show how trade policy and industrial accidents reshape daily costs and safety for millions.
Ep 118: A cyberattack on a major Japanese frozen-food supplier has forced KFC outlets to warn of shortages, showing how one breach can ripple through daily supply chains for millions of customers.
Ep 117: Two U.S. soldiers killed in Jordan mark the first American deaths since renewed Iran fighting, raising stakes for Middle East stability and global shipping routes.
Ep 116: Venezuela's twin earthquakes have killed more than 5,000 people and now require coordinated international reconstruction aid to begin.

Ep 115: A Ukrainian tycoon's accusation that Kyiv's intelligence service tried to assassinate him in Monaco highlights deepening internal fractures that could affect the country's war effort and Western support.

content: Ép 44 : Le déploiement de Starlink V3 par Starship Flight 13 et son amerrissage intact ouvrent la voie à une tentative de capture par la tour pour le prochain vol
Ep 43: Tropical Storm Bertha forces Starship Flight 13 to Friday, extending the test campaign's weather-driven pauses at Starbase.
Ep 42 : Le vol 13 de Starship ce soir testera pour la première fois le déploiement de Starlink depuis la stack complète, faisant progresser la validation du matériel de ravitaillement orbital.

Ep 41 : Le servicer MRV-1 de Northrop Grumman est désormais en orbite après son vol sur Falcon 9, amorçant la première installation en orbite de pods de propulsion qui pourraient prolonger la vie de trois satellites commerciaux vieillissants.
Ép 40 : Le satellite doté d’un bras robotique de Northrop Grumman s’envole aujourd’hui vers l’orbite à bord d’une Falcon 9, faisant passer le servicing en orbite de l’étude au matériel de vol.
Ép 39 : Le 50e lancement de Vandenberg en 2026 montre que la réutilisation de Falcon 9 maintient la cadence tandis que Starship se prépare à son prochain vol d’essai V3
Ép 38 : La cible du 23 juillet de Starship inclut désormais les premiers satellites V3, ce qui déterminera si le véhicule peut fournir des liaisons gigabit opérationnelles avant la fin de l’année.

Ép. 37 : Avancées infrastructurelles au Texas et en Louisiane et 50e vol californien de Falcon de l’année : des pas concrets vers une cadence de lancement accrue alors que les essais Starship se poursuivent
Ep 36 : Des problèmes d’allumage des Raptor lors du dernier test Starship obligent à deux changements de moteurs et repoussent le calendrier de la réutilisation rapide du booster.
Ép 35 : L'échec d'allumage du Raptor sur Flight 13 force un cycle de re-test rapide qui teste la rapidité avec laquelle Starbase peut itérer sur la fiabilité du démarrage moteur.

Ep 34 : La clôture de l’enquête sur l’incident du vol 12 lève la dernière restriction réglementaire sur la démonstration de rallumage moteur de Starship, qui conditionne directement les calendriers de l’atterrisseur Artemis III.

Ep 33 : Le vol 13 de Starship, qui marquera le lancement inaugural des satellites V3, testera si le véhicule peut livrer des charges utiles opérationnelles tout en faisant progresser les objectifs de réutilisation rapide.
Ép. 32 : Le 28e vol de B1080 vise la 600e réutilisation d’un booster Falcon, réduisant encore le coût marginal de chaque kilogramme en orbite.
Ép 31 : Les améliorations des propergols et de l’avionique du Vol 13 rapprochent Starship d’une démonstration de réutilisation rapide qui ferait s’effondrer les coûts de lancement.

Ep 30 : Le vol du 16 juillet de Starship tentera le premier déploiement orbital de satellites Starlink V3, testant directement les liens laser améliorés et la capacité de masse nécessaires à la prochaine phase de croissance de la constellation.
Ép 29 : Le test de feu statique de durée record du Booster 20 reporte Starship Flight 13 sur une cible du 15 juillet et teste les marges thermiques nécessaires à une réutilisation rapide du booster.

Ép 28 : Le déploiement du Booster 20 vers le Pad 2 et l’installation d’une grue de 420 tonnes à Cape Gigabay marquent des étapes concrètes vers une cadence de vol Starship plus élevée et des opérations au sol.
Ép 27 : Le 36e vol de Falcon 9 repousse aujourd’hui les limites de durée de vie du booster et maintient le rythme nécessaire à l’année record de déploiements de Starlink
Ép 26 : Les contrats de covoiturage lunaire de Starship font avancer les calendriers de ravitaillement orbital et de livraison de charges lourdes en démontrant une demande commerciale précoce.
Ép 25 : Une cadence record des Falcon et un nouveau déploiement rideshare montrent comment les marges de réutilisation creusent l’écart entre capacité de lancement annuelle et demande
Ép 24 : Le vol Starlink de Falcon 9 sert aussi de plateforme de test de puces, analysant le comportement des semi-conducteurs sous les charges de lancement.

Ép 23 : Le tir statique complété de Ship 40 et un banc d’essai semi-conducteur à bord du Falcon 9 d’aujourd’hui testent tous deux du matériel qui doit résister à des charges thermiques et vibratoires répétées avant la mise à l’échell
Ép 22 : Les tests des moteurs de Starship franchissent une étape clé vers le treizième vol et la première démonstration de ravitaillement orbital
Ép 21 : Le tir statique à six moteurs de Starship fait progresser la treizième campagne d’essais en vol en validant le groupe complet de Raptors avant les tentatives orbitales.
Ep 20 : Le 1 000e moteur Merlin 1D illustre comment la réutilisation de Falcon a fait des vols répétés le principal moteur des gains de fiabilité des moteurs.
Ép 19 : Un pipeline de gaz de huit miles à Starbase pour lever le goulot d’étranglement des propergols qui limite la cadence de lancement de Starship

Ép 18 : Les réductions mesurées de la masse à vide sur le matériel IFT-12 élargissent la marge de charge utile que le ravitaillement orbital doit combler avant que les missions vers Mars ne deviennent routinières.

Ép 17 : Le lancement sur Falcon 9 d’un satellite SiriusXM de 15 000 livres illustre la cadence soutenue du véhicule pour les charges utiles lourdes, tandis que le tir statique de Starship 40 fait avancer le matériel du Flight 13.
Ép 16 : Le tir statique mono-moteur de Ship 40 passe la première porte hot-fire pour le véhicule qui effectuera le prochain test intégré de Starship
Ép 15 : Le gazoduc dédié au Texas de Starpipe élimine un goulot d’étranglement dans la livraison de propergol qui a limité la cadence de lancement de Starship à Starbase.

Ép 14 : L’expansion validée de Vandenberg et le lancement Starlink d’hier font grimper les compteurs de réutilisation Falcon tandis que le matériel Starship progresse vers des tests de calcul orbital.

content: Ep 552: Tesla's FSD v14.3.6 now pulls into Sheetz entrances and assigned home spots that previously needed manual driving.
Ep 551: Tesla is sending AI safety operators into Colombia and Chile to oversee the first Robotaxi operations outside North America.
Ep 550: Heavy spending on AI, robots and robotaxis is squeezing Tesla's profits even as revenue climbs to a record.
Ep 549: NHTSA's engineering analysis of FSD on 3.2 million vehicles puts Tesla's camera-only system under final scrutiny before any recall decision.
Ep 548: Starlink V5's roof integration in the Cybercab requires a full redesign of thermal paths and pressure vents that would otherwise limit robotaxi uptime.
Ep 547: Tesla's first Semi Megacharger station in California opens the door to commercial long-haul electric trucking economics.
Ep 546: Tesla's LFP batteries retained 93.34% capacity after 62,000 miles, beating nickel packs and shifting long-term ownership math.
Ep 545: Franz von Holzhausen receiving the first protected Model S Signature unit shows Tesla still values its design heritage even as focus shifts to new platforms.
Ep 544: Tesla opens its first public Megacharger in California, unlocking 1.2 MW speeds for Semi fleets.
Ep 543: Tesla’s Model Y robotaxi fleet in Texas grew 50 percent in one day, marking the first visible test of scaled unsupervised operations.
Ep 542: Tesla posted its best second quarter ever as the energy business spiked sharply higher.
Ep 541: Tesla's European FSD fleet passed 50 million kilometers in under three months, handing regulators in Germany and France the real-world data they have been waiting for.
Ep 540: Tesla's Fremont factory teardown signals the shift from legacy vehicles to Optimus production scale.
Ep 539: Tesla's new patent lets GPUs pull only the exact frames needed for training, cutting wasted decode time at petabyte scale.
Ep 538: Fremont's 46-day teardown of the original Model S and X line frees factory space for Optimus production cells.
Ep 537: Tesla's patented breathing glass roof could cut hot-weather range loss by actively managing cabin climate where the sun hits hardest.
Ep 536: A US judge's approval of the $1.5 million SEC settlement ends Musk's personal liability in the 2022 Twitter disclosure case.
Ep 535: Tesla's Gulf Coast lithium refinery will become North America's largest while cutting emissions more than 30 percent versus hard-rock methods.
Ep 534: NHTSA's plan to drop mandatory brake pedals opens a path for robotaxis built without driver controls from day one.
Ep 533: Optimus now targets mass production at Fremont by end of 2026 with a long-term goal of one million units annually.
Ep 532: Strict lease terms left one driver facing $2,141 in wear-and-tear charges after returning her Tesla.
Ep 531: A 379,000-mile 2019 Model 3 in Canada still shows strong battery health, giving owners concrete data on long-term pack durability.
Ep 530: Tesla posted its fourth-best quarter ever with 480,126 deliveries, but the stock still dropped 7.5 percent.
Ep 529: Tesla's new winter heat patent turns the compressor into a deliberate boiler to protect range when ambient temperatures crash.
Ep 528: Tesla plans to add 1,000 workers at its German Gigafactory as June registrations climb in multiple European markets.
Ep 527: Rows of new Teslas waiting in Japan signal a stronger Q3 start than recent quarters showed.
Ep 526: Texas regulators just cleared 84 Tesla robotaxis, the largest permitted autonomous fleet yet and the first real test of scaled FSD operations.
Ep 525: The week's biggest developments, pulled together — what actually moved, why it matters, and what to watch next.
Ep 524: NHTSA ending its power steering probe on 376,000 Teslas clears one regulatory overhang for the company.
Ep 523: Japan's EV subsidies just slashed the price of a base Model 3 to under $20,000 starting next month.
Ep 522: Tesla's dry-electrode patent adds a protective coating to PTFE binder particles to stop lithium ions from breaking them down inside the cell.
Ep 521: Cybertruck becomes the only 2026 pickup to earn IIHS Top Safety Pick+ after avoiding every pedestrian collision in daytime and nighttime tests.
Ep 520: Finland's transport agency is now testing whether Tesla FSD can manage icy roads and obscured markings before any rollout to local owners.
Ep 519: Tesla's $4-5 billion battery storage partnership with NatPower will deploy Megapacks across the UK and Italy to stabilize grids with rising renewables.
Ep 518: SpaceX’s first senior unsecured notes offering marks a shift from equity-heavy funding for its rocket and satellite work.
Ep 517: The week's biggest developments, pulled together — what actually moved, why it matters, and what to watch next.
Ep 516: Hundreds of Cybercabs parked at Giga Texas show production may outpace the regulatory path for unsupervised operation.
Ep 515: Tesla's new lowest-priced Cybertruck trim begins deliveries this week at $59,990.
Ep 514: Tesla's FSD update will remember owners' parking preferences and reduce repeated manual inputs during daily drives.
Ep 513: New Jersey legislation could block true driverless cars, and Tesla is urging owners there to push back before it advances.
Ep 512: Tesla’s Dojo networking patents move packet recovery into hardware so the training fabric keeps running even when Ethernet drops frames.
Ep 511: ABF Freight's order of two Tesla Semis puts the first long-range electric trucks into California linehaul service with routes extending to Reno.
Ep 510: The week's biggest developments, pulled together — what actually moved, why it matters, and what to watch next.
Ep 509: Tesla's foldable Superchargers heading to Europe could cut installation time for new sites.
Ep 508: Tesla Model Y just topped all foreign vehicle registrations in Japan for May.
Ep 507: ABF Freight's order of two Tesla Semis for California routes moves the electric truck from prototype to paid freight work.
Ep 506: Denmark's FSD Supervised approval extends the system to four European countries and shows how regulatory progress can outpace fleet deployment elsewhere.
Ep 505: Multiple Cybercabs at an Atlanta service center show Tesla is moving physical hardware into real-world preparation ahead of any unsupervised launch.
Ep 504: China's 22% Tesla sales rebound in May signals demand recovery after a two-month slump.
Ep 503: Looking back at 8 episodes from 2026-06-01 to 2026-06-07 — the stories that mattered, what we learned, and what to watch next.
Ep 502: Tesla's import of a Chinese-built Premium AWD Model 3 into Canada for under $50,000 tests whether cross-border sourcing can offset domestic production constraints.
Ep 501: Tesla ending free Supercharging for new Model 3s on June 15 removes a key ownership perk just as buyers weigh total costs against rivals.
Ep 500: Tokyo's new EV incentives could nearly halve Tesla prices in the capital region.
Ep 499: Tesla's new interior accent lights now turn red to warn of blind-spot vehicles, giving drivers a direct visual cue without glancing at mirrors.
Ep 498: Halifax gets its first Supercharger site under construction, extending the network into Atlantic Canada for the first time.
Ep 497: China's 39% jump in Tesla wholesale volume signals resilient demand amid intensifying EV rivalry.

content: Ep 69: Uber set out to free drivers from taxi medallions with flexible, well-paid work — and left millions earning below minimum wage in algorithm-driven jobs.
Ep 68: Facial recognition was installed at airports to speed security and catch the right people — then the same systems started watching schools, stadiums, and protests.
Ep 67: Marketed as an indestructible shield against fire, asbestos fibers remained in lungs for decades and triggered a slow epidemic of cancer that regulators could not see in time.
Ep 66: D.A.R.E. placed uniformed officers in classrooms to teach millions of children to refuse drugs, yet repeated evaluations found the program produced little measurable change in behavior.
Ep 65: Plastic bag bans cut visible litter but drove shoppers to buy more trash liners and thicker “reusable” bags that often lasted no longer.
Ep 64: Malcolm McLean’s shipping container slashed the cost of moving goods worldwide — and emptied the working waterfronts that had sustained port cities for generations.

Ep 63: Zara and H&M set out to make runway fashion affordable for ordinary shoppers — and created an industry that now produces 92 million tonnes of textile waste a year while emitting 8–10% of global greenhouse gases.
Ep 62: Governments spent hundreds of billions fixing the Y2K bug, then concluded the threat had never been real.
Ep 61: The Royal Navy cured scurvy with lemon juice in 1795, then quietly lost the remedy as steamships and limes replaced the original practice.

Ep 60: Scared Straight sent at-risk teens into prisons to be confronted by inmates in the hope that fear would keep them out of trouble — and later studies found the programs raised their odds of offending.
Ep 59: The U.S. government paid southern farmers to plant kudzu to stop erosion — and the vine kept growing long after the crisis ended.
Ep 58: Companies adopted game mechanics to make fitness, learning, and work more engaging — and watched users chase points while real progress and well-being declined.
Ep 57: Twentieth-century engineers built dams to power the West and control floods, then spent decades dismantling some so salmon could reach their spawning grounds again.
Ep 56: Platforms promised clean feeds for users and quietly hired tens of thousands of moderators to deliver them, shifting the psychological cost out of sight.
Ep 55: US dietary guidelines urged Americans to cut fat for heart health — and watched obesity climb as sugar filled the gap.
Ep 54: The 1968 National Flood Insurance Program set out to limit building in flood-prone areas but instead subsidized far more development behind levees.
Ep 53: Park managers exterminated Yellowstone’s wolves to protect elk and livestock, then watched the rivers, forests, and beavers collapse in their absence.
Ep 52: The Federal Reserve launched quantitative easing to rescue the economy from another Depression — and ended up widening the wealth gap for a decade.
Ep 51: China's Three Gorges Dam promised flood control and clean power for hundreds of millions, yet its reservoir began stressing faults and destabilizing entire hillsides.
Ep 50: NIST's 2003 password rules tried to make systems stronger by demanding complexity and rotation, yet they trained users to create the very patterns attackers learned to exploit first.
Ep 49: Pediatric guidelines told parents to withhold peanuts until age three — and peanut allergies rose sharply instead.
Ep 48: Mao's China exterminated sparrows to protect grain harvests and instead unleashed insect swarms that deepened the Great Famine.
Ep 47: Smokey Bear urged Americans to stamp out every spark — and turned manageable forests into fuel for megafires that now consume the agency’s budget.
Ep 46: The 1978 Airline Deregulation Act promised cheaper flights for everyone — and produced an industry where four carriers now control roughly 80 percent of the market.
Ep 45: Post-war mortgage subsidies made homeownership reachable for millions of families — and built the car-dependent, racially segregated suburbs that later proved nearly impossible to change.
Ep 44: London's congestion charge cut traffic inside the zone by 15 percent — and shifted the jams and fumes to the boroughs just beyond its boundary.
Ep 43: Automakers recast streets as car space and turned crossing them into a crime, reshaping cities for a century.
Ep 42: St. Louis built Pruitt-Igoe in 1954 as a model of clean, modern public housing for working families — and dynamited the first buildings on national television in 1972.
Ep 41: Eisenhower’s 1956 Interstate Highway Act promised faster travel for all, yet in city after city the new roads accelerated the emptying of urban neighborhoods instead.
Ep 40: Synthetic fabrics promised cheap, durable clothes for everyone — and released trillions of plastic fibers that now reach every human placenta and ocean trench.
Ep 39: A synthetic estrogen given to millions of pregnant women to prevent miscarriage instead caused rare reproductive cancers in their daughters two decades later.
Ep 38: Mosquito nets built to save millions from malaria are instead being cut into fishing gear that empties lakes and leaks insecticide into the water.
Ep 37: Europe and the US mandated biofuels to cut transport emissions, then watched palm-oil plantations clear rainforests faster than before.
Ep 36: Hospitals championed alcohol sanitizers to curb deadly infections, yet everyday overuse may be nudging antimicrobial resistance forward.
Ep 35: Millions of women took hormone replacement therapy to prevent heart disease and stay youthful, until one trial showed it raised their risks of cancer, stroke, and heart attack instead.
Ep 34: Purdue Pharma promoted OxyContin as nearly addiction-proof, yet the drug helped ignite an opioid epidemic that has killed more than a million Americans.
Ep 33: Factories added radium to watch dials so soldiers could read time in the dark — then trained the painters to shape brushes between their lips.
Ep 32: António Egas Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize for the prefrontal lobotomy, a procedure that soon left tens of thousands with lasting cognitive damage.
Ep 31: A sedative promoted as safe for pregnant women in the 1950s produced the largest drug-related birth-defect epidemic on record before testing rules changed.
Ep 30: Europe's GDPR required websites to obtain clear consent for tracking cookies — and produced an internet full of banners that almost no one reads.
Ep 29: Congress set stricter fuel economy rules for cars than light trucks in 1975, and automakers responded by selling millions of SUVs instead.
Ep 28: Daylight Saving Time was introduced to conserve coal and oil, yet modern evidence shows it saves almost no energy while raising heart attacks and crashes.
Ep 27: Western aid meant to build self-sufficient African economies instead left many governments dependent on the next foreign transfer to stay afloat.
Ep 26: The No Child Left Behind Act tied federal funding to test scores to help every child succeed and instead narrowed what millions of students were taught.
Ep 25: Rent control was meant to shield tenants from unaffordable rents, yet it repeatedly reduced the supply of rental housing and raised prices for everyone else.
Ep 24: China's one-child policy aimed to ease population pressure but instead produced a 30-million-person gender imbalance and a shrinking workforce that will shape the country for decades.
Ep 23: Cash for Clunkers paid Americans to destroy nearly 700,000 old cars in 2009 to revive the economy, but it left low-income buyers facing higher used-car prices for years.

Ep 22: Nixon declared the War on Drugs in 1971 to protect families by treating addiction as crime; five decades later the U.S. prison population had grown sixfold while drug-use rates stayed roughly unchanged.
Ep 21: California's three-strikes law promised to lock up dangerous repeat offenders — and instead gave life sentences for stealing pizza and videotapes.
Ep 20: Algorithms built to personalize the internet for every user instead narrowed each person’s view to what they had already clicked.
Ep 19: Wikipedia invited the entire world to write its own encyclopedia, yet the result is an archive that still underrepresents half of humanity.
Ep 18: Ring sold doorbells to keep families safe, but its Neighbors app built a private surveillance grid shared with thousands of police departments.
Ep 17: Engineers built smartphones to put the world's knowledge in every pocket, and created 50 million tonnes of e-waste a year instead.
Ep 16: PageRank was meant to surface the web’s most relevant pages — and it trained everyone to write for the algorithm instead.

Ep 15: Ian Goodfellow designed GANs in 2014 to let machines create realistic images from scratch; five years later the same system was generating non-consensual pornography and fabricated political videos at scale.
Ep 14: Justin Rosenstein built Facebook’s Like button to let friends share quick appreciation — and it became the global yardstick for personal worth.
Ep 13: A designer removed one click to make browsing smoother in 2006 — and helped build the endless feeds that now shape how billions spend their time.
Ep 12: GPS promised to erase every wrong turn, yet it quietly began shrinking the brain’s built-in navigation system.
